questions.title: A library database
questions.text:
A library uses this database.

```text
Members ( MemberID, Name, Phone )
Books   ( BookID, Title, Author )
Loans   ( LoanID, MemberID, BookID, LoanDate, ReturnDate )
```

parts.title: Members and Loans
parts.text: Describe the type of relationship between the tables `Members` and `Loans`.

scheme.mark_scheme: Members (primary key MemberID) links to foreign key MemberID in Loans (1); relation is one-to-many (1)
scheme.model_answer: MemberID, the primary key of Members, is a foreign key in Loans; one member can have many loans, so it is one-to-many.

parts.title: Draw the ERD

nodes.label:
Loans
LoanID, MemberID, BookID, LoanDate, ReturnDate

Correct entities connected (Members–Loans, Loans–Books) (1)
Members 1 — M Loans (1)
Loans M — 1 Books (1)
scheme.model_answer: Members 1 —— M Loans M —— 1 Books

parts.title: Foreign keys
parts.text: Identify the field(s) that can be used as foreign keys in `Loans`, and state what each one links to.

scheme.mark_scheme:
MemberID — links to Members (1)
BookID — links to Books (1)
Do not award a mark if only one field is given without the other.
scheme.model_answer: MemberID links each loan to a member; BookID links each loan to a book.

parts.title: Members and Books
parts.text: Explain the relationship between `Members` and `Books`, and why the `Loans` table is needed.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Members and Books have a many-to-many relationship: a member borrows many books; a book is borrowed by many members (over time) (1)
- an M:M relationship cannot be created directly (1)
- Loans is the link table that turns it into two one-to-many relationships (and stores LoanDate etc.) (1)
scheme.model_answer: A member can borrow many books and a book can be borrowed by many members, so the relationship is many-to-many. This cannot be stored directly, so Loans acts as a link table, giving Members 1—M Loans and Books 1—M Loans, and also stores the loan dates.

- OrderLines is the link table that resolves it into two 1:M relationships (and stores the quantity) (1)

A library lends books to members. Each member has a **member ID**; each book has a **book ID**. Over time a member borrows many books, and a book is borrowed by many members. Each book is published by one publisher (identified by a **publisher ID**); a publisher publishes many books. Use a link entity called **Loan** for members and books.

Draw the ERD in its **final form**: one box per entity with its name on the first line and its **identifier (primary key)** on the next line. A many-to-many relationship cannot be stored, so replace it with the link entity named in the scenario. Select each line and set its degree (1:1, 1:M, M:1 or M:M).

scheme.mark_scheme:
Entities: Member, Book, Publisher, Loan (1 item each)
Identifiers: Member – MemberID; Book – BookID / ISBN; Publisher – PublisherID (1 item each)
Relationships: Member 1:M Loan; Book 1:M Loan; Publisher 1:M Book (1 item each, with the correct degree)
10 items in all; the 4 marks are given in proportion to the correct items. Each extra entity or line cancels one correct item.
scheme.model_answer: Member 1 —— M Loan M —— 1 Book M —— 1 Publisher

questions.title: Build an ERD: orders and products (final form)
questions.text:
An online shop stores customers, orders and products. A customer (**customer ID**) places many orders; each order (**order ID**) is placed by one customer. An order contains many products, and a product (**product ID**) appears in many orders. Use a link entity called **OrderLine** for orders and products.

Draw the ERD in its **final form**: one box per entity with its name on the first line and its **identifier (primary key)** on the next line. A many-to-many relationship cannot be stored, so replace it with the link entity named in the scenario. Select each line and set its degree (1:1, 1:M, M:1 or M:M).

scheme.mark_scheme:
Entities: Customer, Order, Product, OrderLine (1 item each)
Identifiers: Customer – CustomerID; Order – OrderID; Product – ProductID (1 item each)
Relationships: Customer 1:M Order; Order 1:M OrderLine; Product 1:M OrderLine (1 item each, with the correct degree)
10 items in all; the 4 marks are given in proportion to the correct items. Each extra entity or line cancels one correct item.
scheme.model_answer: Customer 1 —— M Order 1 —— M OrderLine M —— 1 Product

questions.title: Build an ERD: a clinic (final form)
questions.text:
A clinic stores departments, doctors and patients. Each department (**department ID**) has many doctors, and each doctor (**doctor ID**) works in one department. A doctor sees many patients, and a patient (**patient ID**) sees many doctors. Use a link entity called **Appointment** for doctors and patients.

Draw the ERD in its **final form**: one box per entity with its name on the first line and its **identifier (primary key)** on the next line. A many-to-many relationship cannot be stored, so replace it with the link entity named in the scenario. Select each line and set its degree (1:1, 1:M, M:1 or M:M).

scheme.mark_scheme:
Entities: Department, Doctor, Patient, Appointment (1 item each)
Identifiers: Department – DepartmentID / DeptID; Doctor – DoctorID; Patient – PatientID (1 item each)
Relationships: Department 1:M Doctor; Doctor 1:M Appointment; Patient 1:M Appointment (1 item each, with the correct degree)
10 items in all; the 4 marks are given in proportion to the correct items. Each extra entity or line cancels one correct item.
scheme.model_answer: Department 1 —— M Doctor 1 —— M Appointment M —— 1 Patient

questions.title: Build an ERD: exam entries (final form)
questions.text:
An exam board stores schools, candidates and exams. Each school (**school ID**) has many candidates, and each candidate (**candidate number**) belongs to one school. A candidate sits many exams, and each exam (**exam code**) is sat by many candidates. Use a link entity called **Entry** for candidates and exams.

Draw the ERD in its **final form**: one box per entity with its name on the first line and its **identifier (primary key)** on the next line. A many-to-many relationship cannot be stored, so replace it with the link entity named in the scenario. Select each line and set its degree (1:1, 1:M, M:1 or M:M).

scheme.mark_scheme:
Entities: School, Candidate, Exam, Entry (1 item each)
Identifiers: School – SchoolID; Candidate – CandidateNumber / CandidateNo / CandidateID; Exam – ExamCode / ExamID (1 item each)
Relationships: School 1:M Candidate; Candidate 1:M Entry; Exam 1:M Entry (1 item each, with the correct degree)
10 items in all; the 4 marks are given in proportion to the correct items. Each extra entity or line cancels one correct item.
scheme.model_answer: School 1 —— M Candidate 1 —— M Entry M —— 1 Exam

questions.title: Build an ERD: car hire (final form)
questions.text:
A car hire company has several branches. Each branch (**branch ID**) has many cars, and each car (**registration number**) belongs to one branch. Over time a customer (**customer ID**) hires many cars, and a car is hired by many customers. For each hire the company stores the start date and the return date. Use a link entity called **Hire** for customers and cars.

Draw the ERD in its **final form**: one box per entity with its name on the first line and its **identifier (primary key)** on the next line. A many-to-many relationship cannot be stored, so replace it with the link entity named in the scenario. Select each line and set its degree (1:1, 1:M, M:1 or M:M).

scheme.mark_scheme:
Entities: Branch, Car, Customer, Hire (1 item each)
Identifiers: Branch – BranchID; Car – RegistrationNumber / RegNumber / RegNo / Registration / CarID; Customer – CustomerID (1 item each)
Relationships: Branch 1:M Car; Customer 1:M Hire; Car 1:M Hire (1 item each, with the correct degree)
10 items in all; the 4 marks are given in proportion to the correct items. Each extra entity or line cancels one correct item.

questions.title: Build an ERD: a cinema (final form)
questions.text:
A cinema shows films on its screens. Each film (**film ID**) is shown at many screenings, and each screening (**screening ID**) shows one film. Each screen (**screen number**) holds many screenings; a screening takes place on one screen. A customer (**customer ID**) books tickets for many screenings, and a screening has many customers. Use a link entity called **Ticket** for customers and screenings.

Draw the ERD in its **final form**: one box per entity with its name on the first line and its **identifier (primary key)** on the next line. Identifiers: Film – FilmID / MovieID; Screening – ScreeningID / ShowID; Screen – ScreenNumber / ScreenNo / ScreenID; Customer – CustomerID (1 item each)
Relationships: Film 1:M Screening; Screen 1:M Screening; Screening 1:M Ticket; Customer 1:M Ticket (1 item each, with the correct degree)

summary: Entities, attributes and relationships; one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many relationships; how relationships are created with primary and foreign keys and link tables; and how to read and draw entity-relationship diagrams (ERDs).

blocks.content: A **thing (person, object, place or event)** about which data is stored — for example *Student*, *Book*, *Order*. Each entity becomes a **table** in a relational database.
A **property** of an entity — one item of data stored about it, e.g. *StudentID*, *Name*, *DateOfBirth*. Each attribute becomes a **field (column)**.

A **link between two entities** that shows how their records are connected, e.g. *a teacher **teaches** many classes*. In a database a relationship is created with a **primary key** in one table and a matching **foreign key** in another.

A diagram that shows the **entities** in a system (as boxes), the **relationships** between them (as lines), and the **degree (cardinality)** of each relationship — one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. It is drawn during the **design** stage, before the tables are created.

blocks.text: Finding entities and attributes in a description

blocks.title: Reading a description like an analyst
items: Underline the **nouns**: the important ones about which **many records** are kept are **entities** (*member*, *trainer*, *class*).
The **details** stored about each entity are its **attributes** (*member's name*, *phone*, *date joined*).
The **verbs** that connect two entities are **relationships** (*a trainer **leads** a class*, *a member **books** a class*).
Choose an attribute that is **unique** for every record as its identifier (*MemberID*) — it will become the primary key.

blocks.title: A gym
blocks.content:
*A gym has many **members**. Each member has a member number, a name, a phone number and the date they joined. Members **book** fitness **classes**; each class has a code, a name, a day and a time. Each class is **led** by one **trainer**; a trainer has a staff number and a name and can lead several classes.*

| Entity | Attributes | Identifier |
|---|---|---|
| Member | MemberNo, Name, Phone, DateJoined | MemberNo |
| Class | ClassCode, ClassName, Day, Time | ClassCode |
| Trainer | StaffNo, Name | StaffNo |

Relationships: *Trainer **leads** Class*, *Member **books** Class*.

blocks.title: Entity, attribute or value?
rows: A **kind of thing** with many records
**One piece of data** in one record

blocks.content: `11A` is a **value** of the attribute `Class`, not an entity. `DateOfBirth` is an **attribute** of `Pupil`. Something becomes a separate entity only if you need to store **several facts about it** (e.g. `Class` with its room and form tutor).

blocks.title: The three types of relationship
rows: Each record in A is linked to **at most one** record in B, and each record in B to **one** in A
Country — Capital city; Person — Passport; Student — Locker
One record in A is linked to **many** records in B, but each record in B is linked to **only one** in A
Publisher — Titles; Class — Pupils; Customer — Orders
One record in A is linked to **many** in B **and** one record in B is linked to **many** in A
Students — Courses; Actors — Films; Products — Orders

blocks.content:
Ask the question **in both directions**:
1. "Can one **Publisher** have many **Titles**?" — **Yes**.
2. "Can one **Title** have many **Publishers**?" — **No**.
One "yes" and one "no" → **one-to-many** (the "many" is on the Titles side). Two "yes" → many-to-many. Two "no" → one-to-one.

blocks.caption: ERD notation — crow's foot and labels
One-to-many: one publisher publishes many titles

blocks.text: Practising the degree of a relationship

blocks.title: Reading relationship sentences
rows: Each pupil has one locker; each locker belongs to one pupil.
1 pupil → many lockers? **No**. 1 locker → many pupils? **No**
A team has many players; each player plays for one team.
A customer places many orders; each order is placed by one customer.
A pupil studies many subjects; a subject is studied by many pupils.
A doctor treats many patients; a patient is treated by many doctors.
Each country has one capital; each capital is in one country.
A class has many pupils; each pupil is in one class.
An author writes many books; a book can have many authors.

blocks.title: Cardinality and degree
blocks.content: Both words are used for "how many records on each side": **one-to-one**, **one-to-many**, **many-to-many**. In the exam, always say **which side is "many"**, e.g. "one-to-many: one class has many pupils".

blocks.title: Symbols used in ERDs
rows: Attributes listed inside or under the box
Its **attributes**; the identifier is underlined or marked **PK**
A **relationship**, often labelled with a verb (*places*, *teaches*)
`1` or a short bar across the line at an end
`M` or a crow's foot `<` at an end

blocks.content: Read the sentence "one **Class** has many **Pupils**": the crow's foot is drawn at the **Pupil** end — the side that has many records for one record on the other side.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Identify two entities in a library system and two attributes of one of them. [3]**
Entities: Member, Book (1 each). Attributes of Book: BookID, Title (1).

**Q: State the type of relationship between Team and Player. Justify your answer. [2]**
One-to-many (1): one team has many players, but each player plays for only one team (1).

**Q: Define the term entity. [1]**
A thing (person, object, place or event) about which data is stored.

- Naming a **value** (*11A*, *Abai Zholy*) as an entity.
- Saying "one-to-many" without saying **which** entity is on the "many" side.
- Checking the relationship in **one** direction only.

blocks.title: How each relationship is implemented
columns: How it is created in the database
rows: The **primary key** of the "one" table is placed as a **foreign key** in the "many" table. *`pub_ID` (PK of Publishers) is a foreign key in Titles.*
The primary key of one table is a foreign key in the other (which must be **unique**), or the two tables are combined into one.
**Cannot be created directly.** It is replaced by a **link (junction) table** whose primary key is usually a **composite key** of the two foreign keys, giving **two 1:M** relationships.

blocks.title: Resolving a many-to-many relationship
blocks.content:
*A student takes many courses; a course has many students.*

```text
Students    ( _StudentID_, Name, Grade )
Courses     ( _CourseID_, CourseName, Room )
Enrolments  ( _StudentID*_, _CourseID*_, StartDate )      <- link table, composite key
```
`Students 1 —— M Enrolments M —— 1 Courses`

blocks.caption: The link table turns M:M into two 1:M relationships

items.title: Why M:M must be resolved
items.content:
- A field can hold **only one value** (atomic), so a student record cannot list all its courses in one field.
- The link table stores **one record per pairing** (student + course) and can hold extra data about the pairing (start date, mark).

items.title: Reading the foreign key
items.content:
- The table that **contains the foreign key** is on the **"many"** side of a 1:M relationship.
- *`course_tbl` contains `StudentID` → one student has many course records → `student_tbl` 1 — M `course_tbl`.*

blocks.title: Describing a relationship (exam style)
blocks.content:
**Q: Describe the type of relationship between tables `student_tbl` and `course_tbl`.**
`student_tbl` (primary key `StudentID`) links to the **foreign key** `StudentID` in `course_tbl` (1); the relationship is **one-to-many** — one student can appear in many course records (1).

blocks.title: Turning an ERD into a relational design
items: Each **entity** becomes a **table**; its identifier becomes the **primary key**.
For each **1:M** relationship, copy the primary key of the "one" table into the "many" table as a **foreign key**.
For each **M:M** relationship, create a **link table** with both primary keys as foreign keys (together usually a **composite primary key**).
For each **1:1** relationship, put the primary key of one table into the other as a **unique** foreign key — or merge the two tables.

blocks.title: A library
blocks.content:
*A member can borrow many books over time and a book is borrowed by many members (M:M). Each loan has a loan date and a return date.*

```text
Members ( _MemberID_, Name, Phone )
Books   ( _BookID_, Title, Author )
Loans   ( _LoanID_, MemberID*, BookID*, LoanDate, ReturnDate )
```
`Members 1 — M Loans M — 1 Books`. Here the link table has its own key `LoanID`, because the same member can borrow the same book again on another date — the pair (MemberID, BookID) is **not** unique.

blocks.title: How to draw an ERD from a description
items: **Find the entities** — the nouns about which data is stored (each becomes a table).
**List the attributes** of each entity and choose a **primary key**.
**Find the relationships** — the verbs that link entities (*places*, *teaches*, *borrows*).
**Decide the degree** of each relationship by asking the question in both directions.
**Resolve every M:M** relationship with a link table.
**Draw** the boxes and lines, marking each end **1** or **M** (or a crow's foot); add the **foreign keys** on the "many" side.

blocks.title: Worked example — a product supply system
blocks.content:
*Stores order products. Each delivery is made to one store and contains one product; a store receives many deliveries and a product appears in many deliveries.*

```text
Stores     ( _Store_code_, Name, City )
Products   ( _Product_code_, Name, Price )
Deliveries ( _Delivery_ID_, Store_code*, Product_code*, Date, Quantity )
```
Relationships: **Stores 1 — M Deliveries** and **Products 1 — M Deliveries**. (Deliveries is the link that resolves the M:M relationship between stores and products.)

blocks.caption: ERD for the product supply system

blocks.title: Worked example — a school
blocks.content:
*A teacher can be the form tutor of one class only, and each class has one form tutor. A class has many pupils; each pupil belongs to one class. Pupils take many clubs; each club has many pupils.*

| Relationship | Degree | Implementation |
|---|---|---|
| Teacher — Class (form tutor) | **1:1** | `TutorID` (unique) in Classes |
| Class — Pupil | **1:M** | `ClassID` foreign key in Pupils |
| Pupil — Club | **M:M** | Link table `Memberships(PupilID, ClubID)` |

blocks.title: Drawing ERDs on the platform
blocks.content: In the diagram questions, add an **entity** for each table (name on the first line, attributes below), connect two entities with a line, then **select the line** to set its cardinality: **1:1**, **1:M**, **M:1** or **M:M**.

blocks.title: Before you hand in an ERD
items: Every entity is a **box** with a **singular** name (*Pupil*, not *Pupils data*) and its attributes.
Every relationship line has **both ends** marked (1 or M).
**No M:M** relationship is left in the final database design — each has a link table.
Each "many" table contains the **foreign key** of the "one" table.
Attributes are **not** drawn as separate entities.

blocks.title: A hospital
blocks.content:
*A hospital has wards. Each patient is in one ward; a ward holds many patients. A doctor treats many patients and a patient can be treated by many doctors; for each treatment the date and the medicine are recorded.*

| Relationship | Degree | Implementation |
|---|---|---|
| Ward — Patient | **1:M** | `WardID` foreign key in Patients |
| Doctor — Patient | **M:M** | Link table `Treatments(TreatmentID, DoctorID*, PatientID*, Date, Medicine)` |

`Wards 1 — M Patients 1 — M Treatments M — 1 Doctors`

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Build the ER diagram for the given Books database (Publishers, Titles). [2]**
Two entities **Publishers** and **Titles** (1) joined by a **one-to-many** relationship, with the "many" at Titles (1).

**Q: Explain the type of connection between the entities. [1]**
One item from the **Publishers** table may have **many** related items in the **Titles** table (one-to-many).

**Q: Draw the E–R diagram for `student_tbl`, `course_tbl` and `courseteacher_tbl`. [2]**
`student_tbl` **1 — M** `course_tbl` (1); `course_tbl` **M — 1** `courseteacher_tbl` (1).

- Putting the "many" (crow's foot) at the wrong end — it goes at the table that holds the **foreign key**.
- Leaving a **many-to-many** relationship without a link table in the database design.
- Drawing **attributes as separate entities**.
- Writing "one-to-many" without saying **which** side is "many".
- Forgetting to check the relationship **in both directions**.

blocks.title: Check yourself
items: Define entity, attribute, relationship and ERD.
Give a real example of a 1:1, a 1:M and an M:M relationship.
Where is the foreign key placed in a one-to-many relationship?
How is a many-to-many relationship implemented in a relational database?
Draw the ERD for: *a customer places many orders; an order contains many products*.
